lead: A refrigerator does not create cold; it moves heat from a cold space to a warmer one, and that costs work. The same cycle with a different purpose is a heat pump: it is the condenser heat Q_out, not the evaporator heat Q_in, that we want. Industry uses these cycles in kitchen refrigerators, air conditioners, cold stores, server rooms and vaccine storage. Liquefaction of gases such as nitrogen and natural gas pushes the same idea to very low temperatures. This chapter builds the vapour-compression cycle, defines its coefficient of performance, compares it with the Carnot limit, and shows how liquefaction cycles are arranged.
prereq: You need the steady-flow device analysis from 3.2, the Carnot COP in 3.3, and refrigerant property tables from Unit 4, Property tables and diagrams.

sections.h3: The four devices of the vapour-compression cycle

blocks.text: Refrigeration keeps a space colder than its surroundings. Heat leaks in, so a device must continuously pump that heat to a warmer place. The vapour-compression cycle does this by making a fluid boil at low pressure, absorbing heat, and condense at high pressure, releasing heat.

A liquid boils at a temperature fixed by its pressure. Lower the pressure, and the boiling point falls. Pick a refrigerant whose boiling point at a few atmospheres is below the cold-space temperature; the cold space then supplies the heat of boiling. The cycle runs in four steps.

items: Evaporator. A low-pressure liquid–vapour mixture boils at constant pressure and temperature, taking heat Q_in from the cold space.
Compressor. Low-pressure vapour is squeezed to high pressure. Work W_in goes in, so the vapour leaves superheated and hotter.
Condenser. Hot high-pressure vapour gives heat Q_out to surroundings and condenses to liquid.

Expansion valve (throttle). Liquid drops to low pressure through a restriction. No work is produced, enthalpy stays nearly constant, temperature falls, and a little liquid flashes to vapour. The cold mixture returns to the evaporator.

blocks.text: For steady flow, neglecting kinetic and potential energy, Q_in + W_in = Q_out. The condenser duty is always larger than the refrigerating effect by the compressor work.

sections.h3: Coefficient of performance and the Carnot limit

blocks.text: Efficiency is a poor word for a refrigerator, because we want heat removed, not work. The yardstick is the coefficient of performance (COP).

blocks.where: COP_R is the coefficient of performance of the refrigerator (dimensionless); Q_in is the heat taken from the cold space in kW; Q_out is the heat rejected at the condenser in kW; W_in is the compressor work in kW.
COP_HP is the heat-pump COP; Q_out is heat delivered to the warm room in kW. COP_HP = COP_R + 1 because the work also ends up in the room.

blocks.text: No cycle between cold at T_C and warm at T_H can beat the reversed Carnot cycle. Its COP depends only on the two absolute temperatures.

blocks.where: T_C is cold-region temperature in kelvin; T_H is warm-region temperature in kelvin. Use kelvin, never Celsius, because the ratio must stay positive and correct.

blocks.text: Real machines reach roughly half the Carnot value: compression is not isentropic, the throttle wastes pressure energy, and heat exchangers need a finite temperature difference. That gap is destroyed work, as in 3.7.

sections.h3: Real cycles, Joule–Thomson expansion and liquefaction

blocks.text: The ideal cycle assumes saturated vapour entering the compressor and saturated liquid leaving the condenser. Practical cycles differ in three ways.

items: The vapour is superheated a few degrees before compression. Liquid droplets damage a compressor, and superheat guarantees dry vapour.
The condensate is subcooled, raising refrigerating effect per kilogram.
Compression is not isentropic; isentropic efficiency is typically 0.7 to 0.85. Use the actual compressor exit enthalpy, not the isentropic one.

blocks.text: The expansion valve is a throttling device: enthalpy is constant across it and entropy rises, so it is irreversible. For most gases below their inversion temperature, throttling also lowers temperature. This is the Joule–Thomson effect, and it makes gas liquefaction possible without moving cold parts.
Liquefaction needs cooling below the critical temperature of the gas, the point beyond which no pressure can condense a vapour, as 3.2 shows.

items: Linde cycle. One compressor, a counter-current heat exchanger and a Joule–Thomson valve. Part of the gas liquefies; cold unliquefied gas returns through the exchanger to pre-cool the incoming stream.
Claude cycle. Adds an expansion engine, so part of the gas expands while doing work. Work removal gives far more cooling per kilogram, so Claude suits large tonnages.

figure.caption: Heat enters at the evaporator and leaves at the condenser; the compressor supplies work. The expansion valve drops pressure and temperature without producing work.

spec.title: Vapour-compression cycle
spec.aria: Refrigerant evaporates while taking heat from the cold space, is compressed, condenses rejecting heat, and returns through an expansion valve to the evaporator.

examples.question: A refrigerator removes 5 kW from a cold space at 250 K and rejects heat to surroundings at 300 K. Its actual COP is 2.5. Find (a) compressor work, (b) Carnot COP between the same temperatures, and (c) minimum work for the same 5 kW.
steps: COP_R = Q_in / W_in, with Q_in = 5 kW and COP_R = 2.5.
Energy balance: Q_out = Q_in + W_in = 5 + 2 = 7 kW, the condenser duty.
Temperatures are already absolute: T_C = 250 K, T_H = 300 K.
The real machine uses 2 kW where 1 kW would suffice reversibly; lost work is 1 kW and second-law efficiency is 1/2 = 0.50.
examples.answer: Compressor work is 2 kW, the Carnot COP is 5, and the minimum work for the same duty is 1 kW.
examples.check:
Q_in = 5.0
T_C = 250.0
T_H = 300.0
COP = 2.5
W = Q_in / COP
COP_carnot = T_C / (T_H - T_C)
W_min = Q_in / COP_carnot
print(W)
print(COP_carnot)
print(W_min)

traps: Putting Celsius temperatures into COP_Carnot = T_C/(T_H − T_C). Take a cold space at −23 °C (250 K) and surroundings at 27 °C (300 K). The correct COP is 250/(300 − 250) = 5. Using Celsius gives −23/(27 − (−23)) = −23/50 = −0.46, a negative nonsense value. The difference 27 − (−23) survives in either scale, but the numerator must be absolute, so T_C = 250 K, not −23.
Forgetting COP_HP = COP_R + 1; a heat pump shows a larger number than the refrigerator it is built from.
Treating the expansion valve as a turbine. It is a throttle: h is constant, no work, and entropy rises.
Using isentropic compressor exit enthalpy when isentropic efficiency is given; the real exit state has higher enthalpy and temperature.
Writing evaporator heat as Q_out. The evaporator takes heat in; the condenser rejects heat out.

quiz.q: Define the coefficient of performance of a refrigerator and state the formula.
quiz.a: COP_R = Q_in / W_in, where Q_in is the heat removed from the cold space in kW and W_in is the compressor work in kW. It is dimensionless.

quiz.q: Why does the expansion valve produce no work even though the pressure falls a lot?
quiz.a: The flow passes through a narrow restriction with no moving part and little kinetic-energy change, so no shaft work crosses the boundary. It is a throttling process with constant enthalpy; pressure energy appears as increased entropy, not work.

quiz.q: A refrigerator works between 260 K and 305 K, removes 4 kW, and has an actual COP of 2.0. Find the compressor work and the Carnot COP.
quiz.a: W_in = Q_in/COP_R = 4/2.0 = 2 kW. COP_Carnot = 260/(305 − 260) = 260/45 ≈ 5.78. The real machine is well below the limit.

quiz.q: A heat pump delivers 12 kW to a room and has COP_HP = 4. Find the compressor work and the COP of the same unit working as a refrigerator.
quiz.a: W_in = Q_out/COP_HP = 12/4 = 3 kW. Q_in = Q_out − W_in = 12 − 3 = 9 kW, so COP_R = 9/3 = 3 = COP_HP − 1.

quiz.q: Why must the vapour leaving the evaporator be superheated before it enters the compressor?
quiz.a: Superheat is used with a dry-expansion evaporator, where refrigerant is fed so that it all boils off and the last part of the coil superheats the vapour; a flooded evaporator wets the whole surface but delivers saturated vapour and needs a separate separator to protect the compressor.

quiz.q: Two refrigerators remove the same 5 kW of heat. Unit A runs between 250 K and 300 K; Unit B runs between 270 K and 300 K. Show which one needs less work, and explain the result physically.
quiz.a: Unit A: COP = 250/50 = 5, so W_min = 1 kW. Unit B: COP = 270/30 = 9, so W_min ≈ 0.56 kW. Unit B needs less work because the temperature lift is smaller; a smaller T_H − T_C gives a larger COP.

quiz.q: State in one line each how the Linde and Claude liquefaction cycles differ.
quiz.a: Linde uses only a Joule–Thomson throttle after a counter-current heat exchanger; Claude adds an expansion engine that removes work, giving more cooling per unit mass.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial refrigeration moved away from chlorofluorocarbons after the ozone treaty, so carbon dioxide, ammonia and hydrocarbons are back in real plants. Absorption refrigeration replaces the compressor with a heat-driven generator and suits free waste steam. Cryogenic liquefaction of natural gas and hydrogen is a large research area; magnetic and dilution refrigeration reach millikelvin temperatures where no gas cycle works. Search next for two-stage and cascade vapour-compression systems, exergy analysis, and the Joule–Thomson inversion temperatures of hydrogen and helium, which need pre-cooling before throttling can liquefy them.
